newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania leaders buoyed by German support for NATO.
newsitem.headline: Romania leaders buoyed by German support for NATO.

text.p: Romanian leaders expressed delight on Wednesday at suggestions that Germany had thrown its weight behind the Balkan country's long-shot bid to win early membership of the NATO alliance.

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, returning from a meeting of European centrist leaders in France, said all participants had backed Romania's inclusion in the first wave of NATO's eastward expansion, due to be announced at a summit in Madrid next month.

Ciorbea singled out support from Chancellor Helmut Kohl of Germany. The United States is one of the countries reluctant so far to back Romanian membership alongside favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

"I had a pleasant surprise to find representatives of all five governments backed our approach and underlined that they will support without reservations Romania's bid to integrate in the first wave," he said at Bucharest airport.

Ciorbea was speaking of his talks with leaders including Kohl, Italy's Romano Prodi, Belgium's Jean-Luc Dehaene, Luxembourg's Jean-Claude Juncker and Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes during their Strasbourg meeting.
There were no immediate details from Kohl's chancellery.
Romania's President Emil Constantinescu, a Christian Democrat, will meet Kohl during a visit to Bonn next month.
"The clear statement made by Chancellor Kohl was new for us. His opinion was very clear in this respect. Bonn had not previously taken a stand on this issue," Ciorbea said.
Romania, where centrists ousted leftists in elections last November, has led a high-profile campaign to overcome the odds against early membership of NATO.

Opinion surveys show overwhelming support among Romanians for quick admission to NATO as a way of removing the post-war division of Europe arranged by the Western powers and Soviet dictator Josef Stalin at the 1945 Yalta summit.
"It's been a major step towards scrapping the legacy of Yalta," Ciorbea said of his talks in Strasbourg.
France, which has longstanding ties with Romania -- the only Latin-speaking nation in eastern Europe -- has been pushing hard for its inclusion in the first wave.

In the run-up to the Madrid summit on July 8 and 9, the Romanian media have whipped public opinion into a frenzy with one private broadcaster running write-in campaigns, lotteries and talk shows spanning several NATO capitals.
Romania cites treaties settling old rifts over borders and minorities with its neighbours Hungary and ex-Soviet Ukraine among latest achievements entitling it to first-wave entry.
Western analysts say Romania is the only applicant with real military punch along with Poland, following its efforts to align its army and equipment to NATO standards.
